intro: The third movement of Mozart’s Symphony No. 40 in G minor, K. 550, is a minuet in three-beat bars, with the winds reinforcing the strings. In the Trio the key changes to G major and the orchestra divides into smaller groups.

sections.label: A · Minuet in G minor, Allegretto
B · Trio, strings and winds, G major
sections.mNote: In the Trio, strings and winds alternate short phrases.

sections.label: A′ · Minuet in G minor returns
sections.mNote: The full orchestra plays the opening accents again.

cues.title: Opening of the minuet
cues.text: The strings begin with a rising, strongly accented phrase, reinforced by winds and horns. The minuet keeps three beats in the bar, and the melody is accented across them.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III, bars 1–14. Marianne Williams Tobias describes the heavily accented opening: https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Imitation in the second strain
cues.text: In the minuet’s second strain, bars 15–42, the string parts enter in imitation with fragments of the tune. The lower strings play against the violins above them.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III, bars 15–42: imitative writing in the minuet’s second strain.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trio in G major
cues.text: The Trio moves from G minor to G major. The strings play a phrase and the winds reply, with the horns joining the exchanges.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III, Trio, bars 43–82. The change to G major is also documented in Tobias’s Indianapolis Symphony note.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Origin of the name “Trio”
cues.text: The middle dance is called the Trio because in the seventeenth century it was usually scored for three instruments. The name remained in use after the practice ended. Mozart scores his Trio for strings and winds in changing groups.
cues.evidence: Harrap’s Illustrated Dictionary of Music and Musicians (1990): the section is known as the trio because it was originally scored for three instruments, a name that survived; Stephen Collins, Classical Music (1997), gives the same account (full-text excerpts seen, pages not recorded). The Trio’s scoring for changing groups: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III.

cues.title: Catalogue entry, 25 July 1788
cues.text: On 25 July 1788 Mozart entered this G minor symphony in his catalogue. The E♭ symphony had been entered on 26 June, and the C major Jupiter followed on 10 August.
cues.evidence: Mozart’s thematic catalogue (British Library, Zweig MS 63), as listed in the chronological table in Otto Jahn, Life of Mozart, trans. P. D. Townsend (1882), vol. 3: K. 543 on 26 June, K. 550 on 25 July, K. 551 on 10 August 1788. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/43413 ; https://searcharchives.bl.uk/catalog/040-001945812

cues.title: Menuetto da capo
cues.text: At the end of the Trio, Mozart marked “Menuetto da capo”, and the orchestra repeats the minuet, bars 1–42. G minor and the heavy accents return at once.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III: the Trio ends with the instruction Menuetto da capo, returning to bars 1–42.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tonkünstler-Societät concerts, Vienna, 1791
cues.text: In April 1791 the Vienna Tonkünstler-Societät gave its concerts, and the programme announced “A Grand Symphony composed by Herr Mozart”, with Antonio Salieri conducting that part. This G minor symphony later gained a second version with clarinets. Both versions survive.
cues.evidence: Otto Erich Deutsch, Mozart: A Documentary Biography (1965), prints the announcement “A Grand Symphony composed by Herr Mozart”; Ivor Keys, Mozart: His Music in His Life (1980), says Salieri conducted that part of the concert (full-text excerpts seen, pages not recorded; the announcement does not name the symphony). The two versions of K. 550, the second with clarinets, are printed in the Breitkopf & Härtel score (1880) and listed at https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.40_in_G_minor,_K.550_(Mozart,_Wolfgang_Amadeus).

transitions.title: Minuet to Trio: G minor to G major
transitions.from: A · Minuet in G minor, Allegretto
transitions.to: B · Trio, strings and winds, G major
transitions.how: The minuet ends in G minor and the Trio begins in G major. G stays the tonic and B♭ becomes B♮. The full orchestra stops, the strings begin a lighter phrase and the wind reply. No passage connects the two sections.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III, bars 42–50.

transitions.title: Return of the Menuetto after the Trio
transitions.from: B · Trio, strings and winds, G major
transitions.to: A′ · Minuet in G minor returns
transitions.how: The Trio closes in G major, and the da capo instruction brings back the minuet in G minor. Winds and horns reinforce the strings again. The change from B♮ to B♭ restores the opening key, and the rising phrase returns with its forceful accents.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), III, end of Trio and Menuetto da capo.

source.title: Mozart, Symphony No. 40, K. 550, Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke VIII/40 (1880), plate W.A.M. 550; parts common to both versions
source.locator: III. Menuetto and Trio, PDF pp. 30–33: minuet, bars 1–42; trio, bars 43–82; then the minuet returns. The edition prints both orchestral versions.

timeline.note: Winds and horns reinforce the strings’ sharply accented minuet.
Strings begin the trio’s G major phrase.
Flute, oboes and bassoons answer the strings in the trio.
Horns join the trio’s exchanges between winds and strings.
The G minor minuet returns, with winds and horns reinforcing the accented strings.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to play the finale through. The work was K. 466 in D minor. It opens with syncopated strings, and the piano enters with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert excellent.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart later dedicated the quartets to him.
